sources.researchNote: The BnF records a male composer and lyricist, born at an undetermined date in the nineteenth century and deceased in 1961, from SACEM information received in 1980; rejected forms are “Charline, Paul (18..-1961)”, a pseudonym, and “Hérembault, André-Paul Roubier d’”. sources.shortCitation: Authority records for Léo Lelièvre fils (1899–1966)
sources.fullCitation: Bibliothèque nationale de France. “Léo Lelièvre (1899–1966).” data.bnf.fr, ark:/12148/cb147911725. Library of Congress. “Lelièvre, Léo.” LCNAF n2010078826. Deutsche Nationalbibliothek. “Lelièvre, Léo.” GND 140364778X. Wikidata Q110225870.
sources.title: Léo Lelièvre (1899-1966)
sources.creator: Bibliothèque nationale de France
sources.researchNote: Two lyricists of the same name were at work in Paris in the 1930s: the chansonnier Léo Lelièvre (1872-1956), born in Reims, and his son Léo Edmond Lelièvre (1899-1966), a member of SACEM from November 1919, who wrote for the Casino de Paris beside Henri Varna and whose covers name him “Léo Lelièvre fils”, among them “Gosse de Paris” (1929) and “Le Tambour-major” from the revue “Paris qui brille” (1931). Both men worked on “Parade de France” in 1934: the Salabert prints of Maïotte Almaby’s créole numbers “La Vraie Créola” and “Ma Goulou Goulou” read “paroles françaises de Léo Lelièvre père”, while the Coda prints of the Jurmann–Kaper songs carry the undifferentiated form. The BnF catalogue is divided over those Coda prints: the notices for the illustrated issues and for the chant-et-piano prints of “C’est chez nous” and “Un baiser de femme sous un ciel de feu” link the son, whereas notices for three further printings of “Un baiser de femme sous un ciel de feu”, including Paul Saegel’s orchestral arrangement, still link the father. The son is preferred on three grounds: the printed “père” used for the other Lelièvre inside the same revue, the continuity of the Varna partnership at the Casino de Paris from 1929 onwards, and the weight of the revised catalogue notices.

sources.shortCitation: Jean Choux on sound cinema — Excelsior
sources.fullCitation: “Les metteurs en scène devant l’évolution du cinéma: Le cinéma, depuis qu’il parle, fait à l’homme et à ses propos une part exhorbitante, déclare M. Jean Choux.” Excelsior (Paris), 25 December 1936, p. 4. With a photograph captioned “Jean Choux dirigeant l’exécution d’une prise de vues.” Bibliothèque nationale de France / RetroNews.
sources.title: Les metteurs en scène devant l’évolution du cinéma: Jean Choux
sources.creator: Jean Choux (interviewee)
sources.researchNote: The photograph carries no photographer’s or agency’s credit, unlike the studio portraits the paper usually printed. It shows the director at work rather than posed: he is crouching beside the camera, giving a signal, with the operator behind him. The interview belongs to a series in which directors were asked what the coming of sound had changed; Choux argues that speech has given man and his words a disproportionate share of the screen.

sources.shortCitation: “Retour des Baléares” — Pour vous
sources.fullCitation: “Retour des Baléares. A bord du navire: Bourdelle, le metteur en scène Serge de Poligny et Jean Gabin.” Photograph. Pour vous: l’hebdomadaire du cinéma (Paris), 9 March 1933, p. 7. Bibliothèque nationale de France / RetroNews.
sources.title: Retour des Baléares
sources.creator: Photographer uncredited
sources.researchNote: The caption names the three men on deck and calls de Poligny the director, without naming a film. The occasion can be identified: in 1933 he directed L’Étoile de Valencia, a French version made for the European branch of Universum-Film, whose story runs from a cabaret in Palma to a ship of the same name, with Thomy Bourdelle as Captain Mendoza and Jean Gabin as the ship’s mechanic. The photograph therefore shows the unit returning from the Balearic locations of that film, four months after the French release of the picture he had made with music by Kaper and Jurmann. No photographer or agency is credited beside it.
